slides.say: A circle with center O has a radius of eight centimeters. A, G, F, E and D lie on the same arc, in that order, and B and C lie on the other arc between A and D. Angle A B F is twenty-eight degrees, angle F C D is fifty-seven degrees, and angle G O E is eighty degrees. What is the sum of the lengths of the highlighted arcs, A G and E D?
So they want the two bold arcs together, A G and E D. We'll find them with the math way, using central angles.
at: So they want the two bold arcs

slides.say: [short pause] Here's the figure again, bigger. To find the length of an arc here, we need its central angle. But no central angle is drawn on arc A G, or on arc E D. So let's draw radii that give us central angles. Let's draw the radius O A and the radius O D.
at: on arc A G, or on arc E D
Let's draw the radius O A

slides.say: Now let's use the givens. Angle A B F is twenty-eight degrees. It intercepts the whole arc A F, made of A G and G F together. We know the central angle intercepting that same arc is twice the inscribed angle. So we'll use twenty-eight to find the central angle A O F.
at: Angle A B F is twenty-eight degrees

slides.say: No central angle is drawn on arc A F, so let's draw one more radius, O F. Now angle A O F is two times twenty-eight. That's fifty-six degrees.
at: Now angle A O F is two times

slides.say: Next, angle C is fifty-seven degrees, and it intercepts arc F D. The central angle on that arc is twice as big. Two times fifty-seven is a hundred fourteen degrees.

That's a lot of givens and a lot of lines. We've used B and C, so let's keep only what we need now. We need the two angles at the ends, angle A O G and angle E O D. We can't find each one alone. But we can find their sum.
at: let's keep only what we need
We need the two angles at the ends

slides.say: The two end angles and the middle angle G O E together make the whole angle A O D. We can also find that whole angle by adding A O F and F O D. Fifty-six plus a hundred fourteen is a hundred seventy degrees.
Now take away the middle angle, eighty. So the two end angles together are a hundred seventy minus eighty, ninety degrees.

Now let's understand why the sum is enough. How is the ninety split between the two? It could be forty-five and forty-five, or twenty and seventy. The givens don't decide it, and we don't need it. Here's only what we need, the angle A O D, a hundred seventy degrees.
Say the middle part, the eighty, sits here, in grey. This is just one possible position. Then the end angles are twenty and seventy, and together they're ninety.

Now slide the whole middle part along the circle, to another possible position. The end angles change, to fifty and forty, but together they're still ninety. Wherever the middle part sits, the two ends always add up to a hundred seventy minus eighty.
Now the length. An arc is a part of the circumference. The radius is eight, so the whole circumference is two pi times eight, sixteen pi.

Which part of it do we need? The two arcs together have ninety degrees. Ninety out of three hundred sixty is one quarter. And one quarter of sixteen pi is sixteen pi divided by four, four pi. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Ninety out of three hundred sixty
Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: When you can't find each part alone, look for the sum. Here it was the whole angle minus the middle part. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: When you can't find each part
